preamble: Prothesis of the labio-velar glide [w] before a word-initial rounded back vowel. It is regular in Upper Sorbian, where Proto-Slavic word-initial *o and *u gained a prothetic [w] (written ⟨w⟩): *oko > woko 'eye', *uxo > wucho 'ear', *onъ > wón 'he'; native Upper Sorbian words therefore do not begin with o or u. Silesian shows the same glide before inherited initial o, written ⟨ô⟩: ôko /ˈwɔ.kɔ/ 'eye', ôkno /ˈwɔk.nɔ/ 'window'. English acquired a prothetic /w/ in one and once from the 14th century in south-western and western dialects; dialectal woak 'oak' shows it too, while alone, only and atone keep the older vowel-initial form. Prothetic /v/ in Ukrainian, Belarusian and Czech (vikno, vokno) is a different outcome and belongs under empty → v.

examples.note: Upper Sorbian /w/ is a velarized bilabial approximant [β̞ˠ].

examples.from: Proto-Slavic *onъ 'he' (cf. Polish on); Proto-Slavic *orati 'to plough' (cf. Polish orać)
examples.note: The glide is regular before initial o and u. It also appears in prefixed words such as wobdarjować 'to reward' (cf. Polish obdarować).

examples.from: Middle English on, oon 'one' (< Old English ān)
examples.note: The [w] arose around the 14th century in south-western and western England and became standard by the 18th century; alone, atone and only keep the form without it.
Middle English already has the spelling wocke.
